projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Morgan Vaux was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Good morning. Today we are with Veteran Morgan Vaux.

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Vaux.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Vaux. And Mr. Vaux served in World War II. He lives in Greentown, Indiana. His street address is 6118 Cloverdale Drive. He was born in Watertown, South Dakota, on July 21, 1918. He served in the U. S. Army Air Core. He was with the American Volunteer Group Flying Tigers, as they are commonly called. He also served in the U. S. Marine Corps. He served in the Air Core from 1939 to 1941. He was in the Flying Tigers from June of '41 to November of '42. And the U. S. Marines from '42 to '45. And he served overseas in the South Pacific area as well when he was with the Flying Tigers along in Burma. Mr. Vaux, if you want to maybe tell us, start with basic training then carry us through your service.

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Yes. Basic training, I think you have it wrong there. It started in September of 1939.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Basic training at Chanute Air Base and Scott Field Air Base in radio operator and mechanic, aircraft specialty. And that was about -- a hell of a training I got. After that it was some field operation, maintaining aircraft, 39th Pursuit Squader. Also working field operations with field radios. That's about it until I was called -- until I got the contract to go to China with the American Volunteer Group. That was when I used my training to be an early warning radio station, station-master.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: That was in Burma?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: That was in China.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: In China?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: In Burma, we were there just from August 1941. I think you had that November or something. August 1941 until August 1942. In Burma, we went there mainly for training, because we had leased -- Chennault and his people had leased from the British Royal Air Force, Kyedaw Airdrome at a town called Toungoo, Burma, north of Rangoon. At that air base the pilots were trained in all kinds of things: landings and takeoffs and maneuvers. They were from the Army Air Corp, the Navy, the Marines. The Navy, Marines had never seen planes we had. They were all new to them. In fact, one man was a flying boat pilot. He had to go from high flying boat pilot to a fighter plane pilot. It took a lot of practice, landings-takeoffs, at Kyedaw Airport Airdrome. That way we lost a lot, wrecked a lot of planes, too. Propellers bent and smashed when they landed the nose over the plane, hit too hard and break the landing gear because they were used to carriers, most of them were carrier pilots.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: The carrier landing you cut your speed and just kind of drop down on the ground, maybe a couple of feet. You can't do that with another type of fighter plane. You have to grease it on more or less on the runway. So, anyway, we lost quite a few planes to start with. There were no replacements. In fact, all during our tour over there we had no replacements to talk about in terms of propellers and tires, things wearing out and blowing out. The only replacements we were able to get were by air by the China National Aviation Corporation. They were flying over the Hump from Chiengmai to India, and they would ferry in spare parts for us. But they had to come all the way across from Ivory Coast, Florida -- Africa. Ivory Coast all the way across. I think they were shipped from there by air somehow. I don't know how they got to India. But our fellas at one time were asked to go to the Gold Coast to pick up about, I think, we got about four or five new model P-40 aircraft. We were flying the original old B-Model, "b" as in baker. At moon (?) we were flying tomahawks. They were new one kittyhawks. They were the E-model, "e" easy. They had bomb racks on them. They had much better firepower. Anyway, we used those few planes to bomb the Japanese Red Dragon Division that was coming up the Burma Road. After they had bombed out Rangoon, everybody kind of got out of there if they could, they destroyed the docks, we moved out of there up the Burma Road. On the way we had to detour at Magee (ph). Over there we lost some men and planes because they, the British Royal Air Force, had radar at Rangoon, Mingaladon Airdome there. That's where two of our squadrons were replaced to help out the RAFs. They had only one squadron there. American Brewster Buffalos weren't very good aircraft. Anyway, they took their radar with them when they moved out. And when we moved out we had no early warning. We had no warning of raids. When we were at Magee, Burma, why we lost several men and planes there due to there were no warnings. So we moved out of there as soon as we could. We had to move to Chiengmai then. We upped the Burma Road. Of course, pilots flew in there with P-40s. Prior to that time we had another engagement with the Japanese from Hanoi French Indochina. They came up on December 30th -- December 20th, 1941. They were headed for - ten twin-engine bombers, they were headed for Chiengmai. They had bombed Chiengmai for years at their liberty, see. They had no protection at all down there. So they came in and we got word of it. See, my radio station was down in an area towards Hanoi. Chennault had also set up a telephone reporting warning system. So he had -- there were Chinese Army Signal Core guys, men down near Hanoi Airport. When those planes would takeoff they would phone up my station. Then the telephone guys talk through my interpreter told me what was going on, what was coming up this way. And I called in to report to headquarters at Chiengmai, and they got word of it in plenty of time. And planes of two of our squadrons hit those ten bombers. Needless to say none of them ever got to Chiengmai. I think all but one was shot down.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Oh, boy.

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: That was a little earlier. That was a first engagement of our Flying Tigers with the Japanese. Then, of course, when the Royal Air Force asked for help down in Rangoon, that's when we got into the big fleets of Japanese coming in over from Thailand. They had bases in Thailand. They'd come over in huge formations, hundred-some at a time. Of course, the British and we didn't have any more than, say, twelve, maybe fifteen planes to go up at a time against those. That's where Chennault's tactics played off by hit-and-run. You hit them, dive off and come back again. That way we saved our men and planes. Shot down quite a few of them, too. But it didn't stop them. They were able to bomb night and day. When they started doing that we had to move out. I think in March of `42 we had to move out to Magee. We didn't stay there long until we had to move into Chiengmai. They made the big record down there right after Christmas time.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: You want to tell again of the strategic importance of the Burma Road.

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Yes. The Burma Road was a supply line for the Chinese at that time because the East Coast docks, all the East Coast harbors, were controlled by the Japanese. The Japanese had the whole East Coast pretty well tied-up.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: East Coast?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: So the only way they could get supplies, maintain their country, was through the Burma Road. And I think our biggest effort we made was we hit what they call the Salween Gorge of the Burma Road. The Burma Road goes across this bridge at this gorge. To get to the other side of the mountain to go on toward Chiengmai from Rangoon. At this time, it was in around May I think of 1942, the Japanese were coming up that road with that Red Dragon Armored Division, a whole division. They were going to sweep up into Chiengmai and that would be the end of Chiengmai, as far as World War II, the Japanese were concerned, they would stop them right there because they would have no way of getting any supplies except by air and that could easily be controlled by the Japanese. They could shoot them all down. So we had three of those late model P-40 aircraft with the bomb racks. We loaded 500-pound Chinese bombs on those racks. I think three of our Navy, former Navy dive-bomber pilots, agreed to make a run on the Japanese lines coming up the Burma Road, and at the same time bomb and destroy that river bridge so they couldn't cross the Salween River, what they called "The Gorge," a big opening there. So they first destroyed the bridge. Then the army column was there, so they knocked -- they bombed against the wall of a mountain and had the mountain come crashing down on the line of troops down below, the Japanese. Then they would bomb the road itself and then strafe, strafe all along there. They did that for several days. The Japanese never got up to Chiengmai. Chiengmai was able to continue the war effort. Let's see. That, I think, it was the crowning effort of the AVG. After that why they never came up that far. After we destroyed their planes December 20th, coming up from Hanoi, they never came back that way either. So our activities from then, from that time on they moved east to airfield called Kweilin. They operated out of there. They made raids on Taiwan. Taiwan was operating under the Japanese. They made raid on the Japanese airfields in Taiwan. Then up farther they had advanced airfields we had made north of Chiengmai, northeast, and used those airfields to attack Japanese airfields farther north. Before we left we were working in the area of the north-northeast China starting with the southwest part of China.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Is that kind of the direction of Burma Road?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Burma Road went northwest up to Chungking, and that was somewhat due north. We did some operating towards the east, towards the ocean, towards the seaports in that direction, large cities. Chungking was kind of northwest somewhat.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: So that was a one-year tour of duty with the Flying Tigers?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: One year. I went around the world on that. I left my home town of Kenosha, Wisconsin, by rail. I went by rail to -- Los Angeles, we met there. About 100 of us met there, various air bases. We took a bus to San Francisco. We got the Dutch passenger freighter at San Francisco, the Jagersfontein, that took us to Hawaii. From Hawaii we picked up two cruisers and escorts because the Japanese had word we were coming, coming to aid the British in Burma. So there was a cruiser Salt Lake City and a cruiser Northhampton. We got escorted to the Dutch East Indies, as far as that went. From there a Dutch cruiser took over and went as far as -- we didn't go as far as Singapore. They dropped off at Dutch East Indies somewhere. We went to Singapore. So then coming home, we had no way to get out of China by ship, India by ship. Had no way of getting over there. So China National Aviation Corporation guys would pick up a few of us at a time, we'd manage to get as far as Karachi, India. In those days Karachi was Indian. From Karachi, India, our ambassador, what they call minister, whatever it is, consulate.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Consulate.

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Consulate was able to get us a trip over to Bombay. We were over there for a while. Then it took about a week before we could get a ship from Bombay, an ocean-going ship. We got a ship of the United States lines called Mariposa. That took us to South Africa, Cape Town, and stayed there a short time. From there, that's where I got my hepatitis showed up there. Up until then it was dysentery. Went from there to New York. Then from New York I took a train to Kenosha. I went all the way around the world on that trip. It was all by civilian boats really. Wasn't any military transport at all. You see, when our time was coming to an end up there in China, we had until July 4th, 1942 was the end of our contract, the Army Air Core sent quite a few people to enlist -- re-enlist us back in the service. They didn't care whether you came from the Marines or Navy. They wanted them in the Army Air Corp. I had dysentery pretty bad. I said "I don't think I can make it." We will make you a first lieutenant if you come. Hell, I left a corporal, left the Army as a corporal. I said "No, I have to get back." They wouldn't give us any time off. You couldn't go home on leave. No place like that. We had to either stay or leave. The head of the recruiting team was a guy named Colonel Bissell. I will never forget that guy. He would not allow any planes to take us out of China. The only way we had to go. No military plane would take us out of China. No military plane could take us from India back home. So, hell, I wasn't about to sign up with that dingbat guy. A lot of the fellas were unhappy with him, especially, and then they wanted to get home after a year fighting out there, living pretty tough. They wanted to get home so they had very few people that re-enlisted. It took us about, I'd say about a month to get there, and I'd say it took a month on the sea to get home. But we spent about three weeks trying to get passage out of India just because of Bissell. I remember two or three of the fellas rented camels. They road around the embassy building there at Bombay trying to influence the consulate, whoever was there, to get us a ship, transportation out of there. They road around there about half a day until they got a detention of people there. It worked out pretty good. In a couple of days we had something. Mariposa, was able to get home on that. Just about all the guys came home that way. But I spent the whole time coming up from South Africa, New York sick bay with hepatitis. Couldn't manage anything. Pretty sick guy. Then I got a sick leave. I got home 60 days. Draft board -- That was another thing. Colonel Bissell said the draft board would be waiting. He would have -- the draft board would draft us as privates in the Army, draft us as Army privates. That's another thing that turned the guys against him. He threatened. Threats given. When I got home the draft board gave me 60-days sick leave before I had to re-enlist. I didn't care about that. I was going to re-enlist anyway.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: You said you suffered from rat bites; is that why you were in China?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Well, after the rat bite, I don't think that had anything to do with that. It was an infection. I still got it on my arm where that sucker bit me. I was looking at that the other day.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Where did that happen, the rat bite, where were you stationed?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: I was at that little place --

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Radio?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: -- radio station. I was using an Army camp cot for a bed. My arm happened to fall down off the camp cot. Boy, one of them got me. It was the hepatitis, I got that somehow over there. A lot of that from poor food, poor sanitary conditions.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: What did you eat while you manned this radio station?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Well, at the radio station, when I moved over there, see, I stopped at Chiengmai Black Dragon Pool Factory. Black Dragon Pool Factory got a Chinese transmitter, it was about a 60-watt transmitter they said, an old receiver that looked like it had been on at the docks somewhere in Indochina. Pretty bad shape. Anyway, it worked. And an old motor generator, put that on the truck. And basically they sent me some canned goods, quite a few canned goods, to last for a while. I was eating that down there at this pagoda where we set up the station. Then the cook decided he would go to the bizarre. We'd go over there and see what they had to buy to eat. Most of it was chickens hanging from wires. We had quite a bit of chicken. Then along with the canned goods, if I ran out of canned goods, I notified the head office up there in Chiengmai, the base, they'd try to get more to me. But I had to pay for that stuff.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: I was given 30 dollars a month extra to be living out there and live with regular meals. They were getting pretty good meals up in Chiengmai. So I had to pay for them.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Were there other radio stations besides yours?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Yes. There was another one down closer to Burma. I forget the name of it. Another one up there closer to Chungking on the Burma Road. Three of them on the Burma Road. Then my first station was south of Chiengmai, down towards Indochina. The one guy had Unanei (ph) on the Burma Road, one station on the Burma Road, they had to give up for some reason, I took over that station. That's where I worked until the end of the tour.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Were these stations based in like civilian areas?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Were these stations kind of kept quiet so the Japanese wouldn't know where they were at? Or were they marked as military?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: I think they were able to know but they were too far away for them to do anything about I think. They didn't think we could do much anyway.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Okay. They never tried to --

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: They had a way probably of checking on the transmission, where it was coming from.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: They never tried to bomb the station or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: They didn't bomb us. They would strafe my station. They would come and strafe my station a couple of times trying to hit planes on the airfield at Unanei. I was up here in a hill, then right down there was a field. They'd come strafing me and then hit whatever they could get down in the airfield. Usually didn't get anything because we didn't have anybody there anyway.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Okay. Well, then, what about your service with the Marines, what was that like?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Marines was a move from one darn island to another. Pack everything, get on a ship and get off. Our main objective, when we were out in the Marines, was to destroy the shipping and the air facilities at a big island base at Rabual, R-a-b-u-a-l. They had a big navy base there. They had an air base there. We had the first Marine B25s. Marines didn't have twin engine bombers until we got ours. They were called Marines PBY --PB (laughing) That was a fine boat. PBJ because it was a patrol bomber they said. We did night bombing of Rabual with radar. I have to make another trip. (BREAK)

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: It was a confusing situation in the Marine Corps because I was trained with Signal Corp Army equipment. The Navy had different equipment. The radio, we had one set of radio, a little what they call a command set in the fighter plane for the fighter pilots to use. With the bombers you had a long-range set of transmitter, a receiver, besides a short range for the pilots. Then they had radar. I had never been to radar school. In fact, at that time the signal core didn't have radar. Navy had started it out at Chicago. So I was promoted to head of the communications of the squadron. I was to be in charge of every part of communication on the radios. So I had pretty much to delegate. I didn't know anything about the radar. We bombed mostly by radar at night. Bombing Rabaul. I think I misspelled. Rabaul, R-a-b-a-u-l. (PAUSE)

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Where was Rabaul at?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Rabaul was in the Bismark archipelago, near the Admiralty Islands.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Near Japan then?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: You would find it by going north probably from New Guinea; that area. It was a big Navy base at Rabaul. They had a lot of anti-aircraft equipment. We even lost the planes at night. We did all the bombing at night. Lost planes and people due to the heavy anti-aircraft they had. We did some strafing of other islands that had some Japanese installations still there, small installations. I went on some raids, strafing raids with them, to see what it was like. Then I just did enough flying to get my flight pay. Usually I would get flight pay ever since I joined the Marines. They give me a 13 tech sergeant rating when I first got there. One step below master sergeant. So I was on flight pay ever since I was in it. But we did mostly that one island. We moved closer and closer to it, moving from -- first we were at Sterling Island North of the Guada canal; then we moved on up to Monda Island. That was in another group of islands, I forget the name of that one, then moved near up to Rabaul, Emmarue. I don't think I have that list of islands that was. Name of the islands. I guess we were pretty effective because they weren't quite -- they weren't sending out fighter planes and raiding around very much after for a while there. We were pretty effective.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Was Rabaul kind of the last campaign you were involved in before the war ended?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Yes. We were out there 1943. Then the war had moved up to the Philippines, up that way. So they moved my squadron north up to the Philippines. That's when they said, well, your time is up. I don't have to go to the Philippines. So I got a hop over to Admiralty Islands. I got on the troop ship, came home that way. Came home a long ways. Still other guys said their time was up. They had time overseas. I think they had Army time, Marine time.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Did your volunteer time count?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: No. It helped toward the service. It helped toward the experience. That's how they figured; I was capable of taking care of communications of the entire squadron. A lot more communications involved in that. Squadron twin-engine bombers, fighter planes. But that was for experience, overseas experience. By the time to go overseas with the Marines, why I got a couple of guys went to the warehouse, we pretty well took care of moving stuff out of the 14 warehouse we needed to operate our squadron overseas. Motor generators and stuff like that we took along that we were going to need. Then we got over there and we found out we didn't have any spare parts. They had mixed Army and Navy radio equipment on the planes. So we didn't have any spare parts for the Army stuff. Luckily there was a fire squadron, a P-38 squadron, over at Sterling Island when we got there. I went over there, found a bunch of parts over there I could use. They let me have them for a couple of bottles of booze. I brought booze over in my foot locker, in my tent where I was with several other guys, when we would have a birthday, I broke out a bottle of booze. I packed it in there with straw and three feathers; lousy booze. So I would use a bottle, go over there, the Army base, trade parts for the planes. Strange story happened when I was over there. It was on Sterling Island. We knew there was another squadron, the other side of the base, Army with P-38s. I never went over there but one time. One night we had a raid -- not a raid, but Japanese search planes were running around one night. We had a blackout. I was in a slit trench there by the tent, some guy jumped in and just about jumped on me. I said, "What the hell are you trying to do?" Turned out to be, it's a strangest thing I ever believed in afterwards. One of our guys in the Flying Tigers, pilot, had jumped on me in the slit trench over Sterling Island and the treasury group out there Southwest Pacific. Of all the guys you could think of how could one guy from that one group over there in China, we were years ago, be jumping into my slit trench. He must have been visiting or something over in our squadron some of our guys. He was from that P-38 outfit.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: It turned out he was from Wisconsin. Years later I drove up to see where he was in northern Wisconsin. He was at a resort or something. I asked him about it. I said, "Remember that time?" He remembered it. But he didn't have much time to talk, he was busy, so we didn't talk much about it. I thought I will see him at the reunions. But the bugger never came to the reunion. All the years I am wondering if it really happened. That guy from our old Flying Tigers squadron would be in a P-38 squadron and jump in on where this Marine Corps slit trench years later. It was about a year after they left China.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: What is a slit trench?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Slit trench.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Just a narrow trench?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Yes, that you have in the ground, we had near right outside of our tent in case a bombing --

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Shrapnel?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Never did happen but we were ready.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: You jumped in there because there was a blackout.

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Yes, blackout. Spotter planes, we never knew a spotter plane when they first started. The airplanes in the vicinity, you don't know whether bombers or what they are. So jump in the slit trench. He jumped right on top. (laughing)

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Is there anything else that you want to add to the tape that you remember? Any other outstanding stories?

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: One of these things that I mentioned. Let's see. Yeah. When I came back in 1945 I was 27. I enrolled on the GI bill at 16 Lawrence College, Appleton, Wisconsin, and I graduated in 1949 with a B. S. degree. Then I went to the Civil Service Naval Electronics Supply Office at Great Lakes. They transferred me -- no, I got a transfer to the Air Force Material Command. I was stationed at Kingston Products in Kokomo as an inspector. While at Kokomo I was hired at Delco Radio, that's how come I came here, as a process and production engineer. So was at Delco Electronics now. Delphi-Delco for 27 years.
[END OF TAPE ONE, SIDE ONE] [SIDE TWO]

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: I don't know if you want any of this stuff.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: I will take that if you want to leave it.

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: This is what I wrote.

sp.speaker: Mark D. Doud
sp.p: Thank you for providing information on the tape.

sp.speaker: Morgan Vaux
sp.p: Yeah.
[END OF TAPE ONE. CONCLUSION OF INTERVIEW]
